beats.headline: Why does Hibernate need a protected constructor?
beats.subline: It isn't just a suggestion. It is the key to how Hibernate proxies your data.
beats.narration: Hibernate uses reflection to instantiate your entities. If you don't provide a no-arg constructor, it fails. But why protected? Because it lets Hibernate build your objects while preventing your own code from creating half-baked entities.

beats.title: The Entity Lifecycle
beats.subtitle: Tracking state in the Persistence Context

nodes.label: Persistent
nodes.detail: Managed by L1 Cache, dirty checking active

nodes.label: Detached
nodes.detail: Database row exists, but tracking is lost

beats.narration: Entities move through four states. Transient is just a new object. Persistent means it lives in the Persistence Context. Detached happens when the transaction closes, and Removed marks it for deletion.

beats.title: The Entity Blueprint

steps.explanation: Marks the class for ORM mapping. Never make this class final, or proxy generation will crash.
Required for reflection. Protected keeps your API clean while satisfying Hibernate's requirements.

beats.narration: Never mark your entities final. Hibernate uses ByteBuddy to create lazy-loading proxies, which requires subclassing. If you block inheritance, the magic breaks.

beats.title: Persist vs. Merge

bottom.label: em.merge(entity)
points: Copies state to a new managed instance

beats.narration: Don't confuse these. Persist makes a new object managed. Merge takes a detached object, copies its state onto a managed instance, and returns that new managed reference.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Never use final on entity classes
Merge returns a new managed reference

beats.narration: That covers the basics. In Part 2, we look at why IDENTITY primary keys destroy your batching performance and how to fix it with sequences.

beats.headline: IDENTITY is a performance trap.
beats.subline: It forces an immediate database round-trip for every single insert.
beats.narration: If you use GenerationType.IDENTITY, you are accidentally disabling JDBC batching. Hibernate needs the ID immediately to manage the entity, forcing it to execute your inserts one by one.

beats.title: Batching Strategy
beats.narration: With SEQUENCE, Hibernate fetches a block of IDs in one go. It assigns them in memory, allowing it to queue up all your inserts and send them as a single batch at flush time.

beats.title: Configuring Sequence Allocation

steps.explanation: Must match your database sequence's INCREMENT BY. If they mismatch, you get gaps or duplicate keys.

beats.narration: Always keep your allocationSize in sync with the database sequence increment. If your DB sequence increments by one but Hibernate expects fifty, you will generate duplicate IDs and crash your app.

beats.title: Batching Configuration
beats.caption: Enable batching in application.properties
beats.narration: Don't forget to set these properties. Ordering your inserts and updates helps Hibernate group similar statements, which is critical for efficient JDBC batching.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In

beats.narration: Now your writes are optimized. In Part 3, we dive into the Persistence Context, L1 caching, and how Hibernate automatically tracks changes without you ever calling update.

beats.headline: Why is there no em.update() method?
beats.subline: Because Hibernate is already watching your every move.
beats.narration: JPA doesn't have an update method because the Persistence Context does it for you. It keeps a snapshot of your entity and compares it against the current state at flush time.

beats.title: Dirty Checking Pipeline
beats.subtitle: How state changes become SQL
beats.narration: When you load an entity, Hibernate stores a snapshot. When you flush, it compares the current entity to that snapshot. If anything changed, it generates the SQL update automatically.

beats.title: Managing Memory in Batch Jobs

steps.explanation: Pushes pending changes to the database.
Detaches all entities from the context, allowing the GC to reclaim memory.

beats.narration: If you process thousands of records, your L1 cache will explode. Always call flush and clear periodically to keep your heap memory under control.

beats.title: Flush vs. Commit
beats.narration: Flush just synchronizes the state with the DB. Commit makes it permanent. If you flush and then roll back, the database discards those changes anyway.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: L1 cache holds snapshots for dirty checking

beats.narration: That's how Hibernate tracks state. In Part 4, we wrap up with schema generation strategies and why ddl-auto: update is a danger to your production database.

beats.headline: Never use ddl-auto: update in production.
beats.subline: It will silently corrupt your schema and lock your tables.
beats.narration: Hibernate's auto-generation is great for local dev, but in production, it is a liability. It can't handle complex migrations and might lock your tables during a deployment.

beats.title: Schema Strategy
beats.subtitle: The right way to manage database changes
beats.narration: Use Flyway or Liquibase for your migrations. Set Hibernate to validate mode. This ensures your Java entities always match the database, without letting Hibernate touch the schema itself.

beats.title: Production Config
beats.caption: The safe way to start up
beats.narration: This is the gold standard. Flyway applies the migrations, and Hibernate validates that your code is compatible. If they don't match, the app fails to start instead of failing at runtime.

beats.title: DDL Auto Modes
beats.narration: Update mode is a guess. It doesn't know if you renamed a column or added a new one. Validate is the only safe choice for production environments.

beats.title: Chapter Complete!
takeaways: Set ddl-auto to validate in production
Never use update on live data
